utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Colonel Poje, if I could remind you of the affirmation which you took at the commencement of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Poje.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: First I would like to go back briefly to a topic that we discussed yesterday, so could we please give to the witness P132. Mr. Poje, could you please -- I would like you to do two things: Could you please take your ruler - we know you have one and we're very grateful that you do have one. What I would like you to do is the following: When we discussed yesterday the position of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade from the Dubac-Zarkovica sector to the Komolac-Rijeka-Dubrovacka sector, so I would like you to measure the length of that position from the south-east, Dubac-Zarkovica sector, via Bosanka, Strincjera, to Rijeka Dubrovacka where you can exactly see it. The position goes down to Rijeka Dubrovacka at Cajkovici. So could you please tell us the length of that position to the extent that that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me again the location up to which I am to measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From the southern side we're talking about the Dubac-Zarkovica sector; Dubac-Zarkovica. Then you go to the north-west through Bosanka, Strincjera. You see that's the position of the 3rd Company. And then you go north-east, and at Rijeka Dubrovacka you see the position at Cajkovici north-east of the position of the 3rd Company. You're going north-west, but we want you to go north-east. North-east on the southern bank of Rijeka Dubrovacka, east. Go to the east and now to the southern position, that position. From that position through the Strincjera position up to the Zarkovica position. These are positions of the 3rd Battalion. So please could you measure the entire length of the position. Do you understand, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you telling me to follow the actual curve of the position, the curved line?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, also the depth of the deployment of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. If we follow the deployment line of the units, the defence units, from Zarkovica where the forward post would be to the last position, the length of that position would total 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's also possible that there is a percentage of error, but it's approximately 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at the next document now. This arose from yesterday's cross-examination. We don't have the translation, but it's a very short segment that we would like to look at. We will have the document translated as soon as possible. What I would like to ask you, Mr. Poje, is to look at item 321 in the document to tell us and to confirm it -- to compare it to your rules of the battalion, if possible, and to tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. Since this is not in English and we've just been handed the document, could someone please identify what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Yes. I was just about to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, is this a document that we looked at yesterday, a document from the rules of the battalion, item 321, or paragraph 321?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photocopy of pages 164 and 165 is a copy of a page from the rules of battalion rule book. So that is that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So that is that -- a page from that document? Could you please answer by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In that document, in paragraph 321, there is this first sentence which states --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "The width of the Defence of the battalion can range from 3 to 5 kilometres."

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender this document as a Defence exhibit, and once again I apologise because the English translation has not been done yet, but we will do the translation as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that be -- could that remain as an exhibit for identification until we receive the English translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For what reason, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So we can take a look at it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can take a look at it after it's an exhibit. It's been identified. We know what it is. Your only worry is you can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it should be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D85.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also please distribute document -- the next document. It is the same -- this document has the same origin. We discussed it yesterday. The witness responded to questions based on this document. It is page 100 and 101, paragraph 200 of the rules of the battalion, and I would like Mr. Poje to just confirm whether this is a document from the rules of the battalion and if this is indeed paragraph 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did we not discuss that yesterday when we talked about the rules of attack?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photocopy of the page given to me is from the rules of battalion book, and in paragraph 200 it is -- paragraph 200 does mention the topics that we covered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And this paragraph 200, or a part of it that refers to the battalion firing group, is something that you also used in drafting your own report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document also as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D85 -- I mean D86. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, I would now like to go back to your report. I would just like to cover some part of your report -- some parts of your report very briefly. First, could we look at page -- page 23 in the B/C/S version, and to explain to us this second sentence on that page, where it says: "The commander of the battalion has the sole right of command over the battalion and all the attached units." What does that mean in practice?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I have also the addendum attached to the report, could you please tell me the paragraph title.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The title is "Command and control," and then we're talking about the doctrine of the use of the battalion, and then in bold we have the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sentence which states: "The battalion commander has the sole right of command over the battalion and all units attached to it in order to carry out attacks." So could you please explain the rights and the duties of the commander of the battalion pursuant to this rule, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the unit, in this case the commander of the battalion, commands the battalion and all the units which comprise that battalion and all the units which were attached to that battalion in order to carry out its combat tasks. And that is why I stated what the commander is specifically responsible for; the correct work of the battalion command and all subordinate officers, the moral and political situation, security, combat readiness, level of training, correct use of the unit and completion of the given task.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All these tasks that you mentioned, as it is stated in your report, are the exclusive right and duty of the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as -- if we're talking about the battalion, then yes, the commander of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move to question 17 in your report. This is on page 27 of the B/C/S version. This is the part that refers to the use of fire support and support for an attack on a populated area. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: First I would like you to tell us if in this part you deal with regulations regulating attacks on a populated area.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Theoretically -- theoretically, it deals with support for an attack on a populated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 27 and the next page, 28, you talk about the factors which affect attacks on a populated area, and you mention from the factors that influence it, the size of the populated area, the difficulty in discovering targets in this populated place, limited visibility, greater possibility of greater enemy activities. All these factors are mentioned in your report.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Mr. Poje, how do these factors influence combat operations that we're talking about? How do these practical difficulties that you mention affect the combat operations? For example, limited, restricted visibility, what is the effect of that factor on the attacking forces in a certain situation?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a unit is attacking a populated area, the choice of targets is relatively difficult because targets can be behind buildings, they can be in parks. Depending on the configuration of the populated area, it's very difficult to find targets, because it can be anywhere in that area. And if we take into account the configuration of the area, the size of the area, the buildings in the area, whether they're large or high buildings, this makes observation more difficult. So in any case, combat operations, and if we're talking about an attack here, would precede under difficulty than they would in normal manoeuvring terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All these factors that you're talking about -- for example, when we talk about mortar fire, do all of these factors increase the possibility of error in mortar fire? Do they have an effect on that aspect?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effectiveness of mortar fire to a large degree depends on whether we see or do not see the target that we're firing at from the observation post. So we must pay a lot of attention to our choice of observation posts so that we are able to see where the target is and so that we can direct the fire of the mortar units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the use of mortar fire in such situations as one of its consequences can have a larger expenditure of ammunition in order to neutralise the target. If we're talking about targets that are under cover or are between or behind buildings or in a park or similar circumstances; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ammunition expenditure tables also provide for cases when we're talking about a covered or a partially covered target, and in principle we always kept to those values. Also, group firing can be stopped before all the shells are fired if we conclude that a target is neutralised. Also, if a target is not neutralised, it's possible to prolong firing on that target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if a target, a covered target, in a populated area is not neutralised but continues to fire on the units, does that mean that the value of ammunition expenditure can exceed the ones given in the tables in your reports as the values given for ammunition expenditure in order to neutralise a fire position to a certain degree?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of shells or projectiles required to neutralise a target is taken from the tables that we looked at yesterday. The unit commander, the battalion commander can decide to neutralise that target with a fewer number of projectiles than stated in the tables, but in that case, the commander of the mortar battery must warn that reduction in the number of shells can reduce the effectiveness of the firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand my question. If the spent ammunition, according to the tables required to neutralise a certain target in certain percentages, for example, up to 25 per cent, and this target is not neutralised but continues to fire on the units of the other side, does that mean that the commander or the commandant must use additional quantities in order to achieve his original objective which he did not manage to fulfil because the target was not neutralised to the extent or percentage planned and ordered?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the target is not neutralised, meaning that it continues to operate, the battalion commander can decide to repeat group firing on that target until the desired effect is achieved, or a decision can be made to neutralise the target in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In addendum 1 and in addendum 2 to your report -- the question is a general one, so you don't really need to look at the document right now -- when you did your calculations, did you take into account the fact that these are objectives, targets that are within a populated area, a built-up area, that fire was being opened at JNA positions from firing positions within a populated area?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There is no factual basis for the statement he just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do you allow me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you posing --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, at the very outset, as can be seen in line 9 or, rather, page 9, line 12, I mentioned addendum 1 and addendum 2. In addendum 1 and in addendum 2. And the entire list of potential targets, the Prosecutor provided a potential list of targets that can be firing positions fired at from the -- at the JNA from the town of Dubrovnik. In addition to that, I am totally surprised by this objection. It would suffice for my learned friend to look at his own exhibits. Let him look at 159, 160 -- P159, P160. The other day we talked about so many potential fire targets within a built-up or populated area. The positions of the Croatian side in the town of Dubrovnik. I am truly surprised by this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, if you'd listened to my few words at the beginning of what you've just submitted, you would have answered me yes and we would have gone straight on with your question. I asked whether you were posing this as a theoretical question, and that is the answer is: Yes. Just as all the Prosecution evidence on this point was theoretical. So please carry on with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not dealing with fact but with postulating a theoretical possibility, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So can you answer my question, Mr. Poje? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. My question is the following: When you did your calculations, those provided in addendum 1 and in addendum 2, did you take into account the fact that these are targets that are within a populated area, and did you take into account the needs and difficulties that those firing from a firing position would have when trying to neutralise the targets that are mentioned in your report, all of which are in a populated area?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I looked at possible positions around the Old Town; Ploce, Bogisica Park, et cetera. And also when I looked at the dispersion patterns, I bore in mind the fact that we are talking about a populated or built-up area, that observation is made more difficult, and therefore the fire executor, the one directing the fire and controlling the fire, one would have to look at the broader area and to take all of that into account, namely, the place from which he can see that target the best, or he would have to locate the closest visible point, the one that is closest to that target, so then he can use that for orientation if that is close to the unit that is operating against them. For example, if I do not see a mortar that is firing, I can locate it by being, say, ten metres away from that tall tree, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If an observer or a gunner from a firing position cannot see and if there is no way for him to see the target engaged, did you take into account the fact that in that case imprecision goes up as well as ammunition expenditure? If you took into account -- if you did take this into account, where can we see it in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I calculated the dispersion pattern. I would have to point out once again that when looking at the initial elements of targeting, they contain accidental errors, systematic errors, flagrant errors I do not take into account now, and all these other conditions of firing if we did not take them into account initially. In that case, the first hit can significantly deflect from the desired target. Once the projectile falls, all these errors can be ignored. Now we have one single mistake; the vector from the target to the actual point of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that later.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When calculating the dispersion pattern at 2.500 metres, the dispersion pattern is always the same, no matter whether it's in a populated area or in a meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that later. On page 28 of your report, there's another assertion about the necessity of partially destroying buildings and other facilities. Please tell us what that means, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you just guide me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Page 28, the fourth line from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a problem. If you could give me --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It is 17(a), and it says: "Indirect fire --"

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I see. I can find it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does this mean, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a building or another facility makes it impossible to open fire and if there is an important target behind it, in that case if such a building is fired from, that kind of building can be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please move on to page 29. It is Provisions of the International Law of War.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of this paragraph, under (B), you mention the topic of an open city. When is a town proclaimed to be an open city?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I would be telling a lie if I would say what place is considered to be an open city. I believe that that is a city against which no combat operations would be taken, but I'm not making any claims because I really am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So as for this section -- Provisions of the International Law of War, that is something that is contained in your report but you cannot tell us anything about this?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer. When I wrote my report, I used the literature I mentioned here, that is to say, regulations on the application of rules of international law of war in the armed forces of the SFRY. So the application of humanitarian law, and that is when I explained this, that -- that such buildings can be destroyed or partially destroyed only if the situation is the way I described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since this is not your own line of work, why did you put it in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the questions that I got was that, and that is why I dealt with it very briefly, just a little. I simply wanted to say that the Yugoslav People's Army observed rules that are contained in international law of war, that's all, and that cadets and all attendees of courses were taught to observe the international law of war and humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The point is contained in the last paragraph of section (b), that is to say that cultural heritage, if it is used for military purposes, will not be considered protected and may be attacked and used for -- if it is being used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that in some other way an attempt should be made to stop operations from such buildings, but I think that if this cannot be stopped, then anybody would have the right to engage such a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: For example, a building where the staff of defence or attack is, is that also a military objective? For example, a building where the headquarters of a brigade are, for instance, is that a military objective?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that from such a building one does not open fire, I would not include it as a target for military engagement or targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What would you do with a building where the communications centre of the other side is? Would that building be a military objective, a military target?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the one hand we could say yes because communications function with the assistance of that centre. On the other hand, if it is a protected city and if there is no military activity coming from it and if there is no direct jeopardy for the other side, then I would not consider that building to be a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm not asking you about a protected city, I'm asking you about a building in which the communications centre of the enemy is. So is that building a military target, a legitimate military objective?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, a building that is used as the communications centre is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was asked what the JNA regulations are. He quoted the JNA regulations. We're getting into legal issues. In fact, right now NATO is being sued over the issue as to whether or not the communications centre or the radio centre in Belgrade was in fact a military objective, and that hasn't even been litigated. That hasn't been litigated yet at this time, and to ask a military artillery expert these legal issues I think is beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be beyond the scope of any of us, Mr. Petrovic, but the legal issue has a relevance to your case. The regulations of the JNA has a relevance to your case. I think this witness can deal with the latter but not the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, my question is the following: According to the military regulations of the JNA, a building in which a communications centre is of the enemy side, is that a legitimate military objective?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness's other microphone please be turned on and could he be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: According to JNA regulations, the building in which the enemy headquarters are where the commander of the operations is, is that a legitimate military objective?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that according to JNA regulations it is forbidden to use cultural monuments for military purposes; not only the monuments themselves but also the area in their immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, cultural monuments, humanitarian facilities, et cetera, are not used for military purposes, and targets are selected in such a way so as to be as far away as possible from such cultural monuments and humanitarian facilities lest such facilities or buildings be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us try to summarise this now. Is it forbidden to use the building itself and the area in its immediate vicinity in view of the fact that in such a way the mentioned building can be endangered?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. Once again we're really outside of JNA regulations. JNA regulations does not deal with the use of cultural buildings for -- the use of cultural or religious buildings or scientific buildings for military targets. That's more of the issues of proportionality and we're into international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My reaction, Mr. Petrovic is that you're now at the point of the content of what you would be submitting this Trial Chamber ought to hold rather than it being in any way relevant to learn what this witness might think. The issue will be what this Trial Chamber will come to hold having heard your submissions on the law in light of the facts. So if the facts are that a protected building was being used for a particular purpose, there will be a legal question whether that purpose was a military purpose, and then the question, if it was, will be whether or not it was a permitted target or a violation, et cetera. Those are all legal issues, and the opinion of one artillery officer about them is not going to help the Tribunal. We look forward to your submissions on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the reason why I mentioned this is that that subject was dealt with in the report that is under discussion. Secondly, all the questions that I put I did put about JNA rules. The third reason is, for example, document P116 that the Prosecutor tendered during Jokic's testimony precisely deals with this subject that we are discussing now, so my colleague Mr. Weiner can see this for himself if he wishes, but I fully abide by what you said, Your Honour, so I share your view that an artillery officer was not supposed to deal with matters related to international law of war, so I will move on to the core of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I make it clear that if you want to learn from the witness whether there were regulations of the JNA dealing with the topic and what they were, please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then I'm going to put another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, do you know that an integral part of the regulations in the JNA which deal with this question of the protection of cultural monuments is -- are documents that are contained in the rules on the application of international law of war in the armed forces of the SFRY? These rules are from 1988, and that this contains all the instruments that we have referred to just now, that they are an integral part of the legal system that was applied in the JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I'm not a lawyer and since there was such a question that had been put, I looked at these rules and regulations. I looked at the regulations of the application of international law of war and the SFRY in 1988, and as a matter of fact, I quoted that, and I quoted the order on the application of these rules. Since I am not a lawyer, I did not go into this issue in great depth or in great detail. I dealt with it approximately on a page or so, I just gave some facts. And I wish to confirm in this way that the Yugoslav People's Army did observe international regulations contained in the law of war, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, thank you. Let's move on to page 30 of the B/C/S version, paragraph 18. So it is page 30 in the B/C/S version, question 18 or paragraph 18(b), "Weapons used to attack Dubrovnik." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, under (b), yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your conclusion is that as far as firing at targets in the Old Town of Dubrovnik is concerned, that targets that are on Stradun were supposed to be fired at with 9K11 rockets; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The first sentence is: "Bearing in mind that the Old Town of Dubrovnik is very densely populated, that it has narrow streets and squares, the widest street being Stradun, and that it is surrounded by ramparts, weapons that can be seen from the weapon emplacements would be targeted directly with 9K11 anti-tank rockets and 20-millimetre cannon." Isn't that written in your report, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not say that Stradun can be seen from the firing position. I just said that Stradun is the widest street in the Old Town of Dubrovnik, and I wanted to say that basically the town has only one bigger open space and that all the rest are tiny, narrow streets. I did not say that there was anything on Stradun that should be targeted by Maljutkas or that Maljutkas should be used to fire at Stradun for any reason. I just said that Stradun was the widest area in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, that is simply not correct, because what you say here when referring to the Old Town, saying that targets in the Old Town can be observed only in Stradun, these targets that are visible in the Old Town would be engaged by direct fire.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they could be seen from the place where the artillery pieces are. I can read what I read once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So let us summarise. If there were a target on Stradun and if that target could be seen from the observation post, that target should be engaged by a 9K11.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from the observation post, from the position of the artillery piece itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if there is a target on Stradun and if the target on Stradun can be seen from the place where the artillery weapon is, then a Maljutka 9K11 should be used to fire at it?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If from the place where a Maljutka rocket is fired you can see the target, then this rocket would be used. Otherwise, I have no way of using it and engaging any such target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If there was a target in Stradun visible from the 20-millimetre gun emplacement, then this gun should be used to neutralise this visible target on Stradun?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said also that if a target cannot be seen from the weapon emplacement and it is in Stradun, then 82- and 120-millimetre mortars should be used.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be used for indirect fire, also under an assumption that the target was on Stradun, which is not what I claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not claiming anything either. I am just discussing your report. Therefore, if a target is in a part of the Old Town that you cannot see from the observation post or from the weapons emplacement, then this target should be engaged by 82- and 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, one should secure that there is a visible target from the observation point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: However, if you cannot see a target in the Old Town from an observation post and it's not in Stradun street, then in that case, 82- and 120-millimetre mortars should be used.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the location from which fire is being opened at the unit is known, then it is possible to use them in order to neutralise this target. I refer to 120- and 82-millimetre targets. If fire is coming from any other part of the town - a park or any other street - and this location is known, then one should first attempt to find an observation post from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which you can see and you can be more effective by firing at such target from 120- and 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just to make it short, the answer to -- your answer to my question is yes?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Item (c), "Control of fire support." So we are still talking about question number 18. Here you say that the battalion commander is responsible for control of fire support. Could you please look at your report and confirm that this is what you said and that this is your viewpoint on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your answer was yes?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph (d) concerning with -- concerning the situation in which you assume that if there was no order to attack the Old City, then that means that the whole system of command or chain of command at the level of battalion has broken up. We understand what is the battalion command, but we don't know what a higher level is that you refer here.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the 3rd Battalion was part of the 3rd Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the 3rd Battalion and that its higher level command should be at the level of the corps within the 9th Naval Sector and that the higher command, as to the 9th Naval -- the 2nd Operation Group?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is irrelevant which command is superior to the battalion. I was talking to the next level of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about immediate higher command?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph (e), possible firing position and deployment of the JNA forces. We're also talking about question number 18.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Here you say specifically, speaking about mortars, that there are three or, rather, two potential firing positions of mortars relevant for the time that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cited those positions that were marked on the map and that refer on the 2nd of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you are talking about mortar positions in Uskoplje sector and about mortar positions or, rather, 82-millimetre platoon -- mortar platoon in the sector of Ivanica. Why when you made your addendum number 2, why did you choose completely different positions of the JNA with regard to the ones that you concluded in your main report that were the positions of JNA mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I prepared my main report, I used the map that we mentioned here, and in that map these positions were marked that I mentioned in my main report. Later, when I tried to make a calculation, and we established yesterday that 82 millimetres of infantry companies of the 3rd Battalion were not entered into the map but they were an integral part of this motorised company, I decided, without knowing whether they were in the map or not - because according to the map they were not marked there - I just started from an assumption that 82-millimetre mortars were with the company, and just in case and theoretically, I calculated the scenario in which -- scenario of what the dispersal pattern would be had they acted or operated from that area, because this addendum was drawn up after I finished my main report and after I had analysed. For instance, the battalion that we mentioned yesterday, and that is the 5th Battalion, we have company firing positions marked on the map, and so I assumed that the 3rd Battalion also had such companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you analyse this position at Ivanica? Why there were no calculations referring to this position?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the symbol of a mortar platoon, we can see that it's not directed towards the city of Dubrovnik but, rather, to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As I understand, under question 18 you talk about the targets that could have been inside the town of Dubrovnik or, rather, the positions from which they could be targeted.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the Old City of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But in your main report, you mention the mortar platoon in the sector of Ivanica. Why are you telling us different today? Why did you mention a mortar platoon in the village of Ivanica at all if they were not aiming at the Old Town or the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned these mortars because they were in the defence area of the 3rd Battalion, and they were located between the front defence line and the command post or the battalion fire group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean mortars? How can they be aiming at another direction than the one where the company is deployed that they are part of? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I look at the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be given evidence -- Exhibit P132.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at mortar positions in the area of Ivanica village. Can you see them?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that these mortars -- how do you interpret the position of these mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first I thought that these could have been 3rd Battalion mortars. Later, by looking at the symbols that signify the platoon firing positions, one could even say that this mortar platoon was part of defence. Later, when I started my calculations of dispersals, I believe that from this particular position there was no fire open at the general or -- area of the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yet you put this in your report.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, once I had analysed the map, at first it seemed to me that this 3rd Battalion mortar platoon was there. However, when I looked more closely at the symbol of the mortar platoon, I saw that symbol indicated that it was aiming outside the area of Dubrovnik, which means that most probably it did not engage targets around Dubrovnik and the town of Dubrovnik itself. That is why later I did not take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So that is a mistake in your basic report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that my initial assessment was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your basic assessment on which you compiled and wrote your report.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it essentially affects my report, the fact that these particular mortars were not used to target the area of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And now let's move to the conclusion of your report. These are questions 20 and 21. In the first paragraph, the first item about 120-millimetre mortars, first of all, let's clarify. Yesterday, we agreed that 120-millimetre mortars with active-reactive shells for the most part were not located in the area that we're talking about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most probably that is correct. I'd never had access to firing tables dealing with active-reactive shells, so probably these types were not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The second type of shell that you talk about is the light contact shell.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When we take into account this paragraph where you talk about 120-millimetre mortars and -- and your definitions of possible firing positions from section (e) of question 18, can we conclude, based on that, that it was possible to launch 120-millimetre mortar fire from the position of Uskoplje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I think yesterday we concluded that the firing distance from Uskoplje to the closest possible facility on the map is 5.600 or 700 metres, the range of the light artillery is up to 6.000 or -- 6.400 or 6.500 metres. So it's possible. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude that the only possible position of the 120-millimetre mortar in your report is the position of the 120-millimetre mortars from the firing group at Uskoplje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm speaking exclusively about the positions at Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The answer is yes then?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about 82-millimetre mortars, you state here that 82-millimetre mortars could reach half of the Old City of Dubrovnik, including Stradun. So in your report, you note that 82-millimetre mortars had a range in the northern part of the Old City and -- they had that within range and that the lower boundary was Stradun, which goes from east to west. Is it correct that this is stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And that is your conclusion on the lowest boundary of the range of the 82-millimetre mortars in view of the JNA positions at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, could we now go back to something which is in the addendum -- addenda 1 and 2 to your report where we are quantifying or clarifying the values for Vd and Vp.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your report, in addendum 1 -- excuse me for just a moment. This is something in paragraph 12, question 12, and it refers to the different factors in the effective firing range. So in 12, you note -- the last paragraph of question 12 is that the least favourable conditions for firing are when the target is on the backward slope; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So now could you please look at P10, Exhibit P10, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, could the witness please have a piece of paper, and could he draw the example of a backward slope of a firing -- of a firing target.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the configuration of the terrain where the weapon is where I have drawn it. Let's assume that here, with a triangle, we mark the observation point. The target can be on the facing slope at the top or at the rear slope. That is the target. I have marked it a little more in bold. And then we have the direction of the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, could you please mark the mortar position with the letter A.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: With B, could you indicate the observation form.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And with a C can you mark the target on the rear slope.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the effect of the target being on the rear slope on the dispersion ellipsis from a projectile fired from position A?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispersion increases with the increasing slope of the terrain. So the greater the slope, the greater the dispersion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how the cluster goes, the direction, and how it spreads.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could draw a dispersion ellipse now for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the difference between an ellipse on flat ground where the target is or of the dispersion ellipse of a target which is on a backward -- back slope or rear slope?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispersion pattern is greater if we have a rear slope. The dispersion pattern will increase with the increase in the slope degree, but the dispersion will not be changed by the type of weapon that is being used. For example, 105-millimetre or 122-millimetre. It is affected, though, by the slope.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So when we're firing on a target on a rear slope, the dispersion pattern is much greater than an ellipse of dispersion of an artillery weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. You misunderstood the answer. You have it the other way around. I didn't say that. I said that the dispersion pattern on a rear slope, when we use mortars, due to the characteristic of the trajectory in vertical firing, the dispersion pattern on a back slope is smaller than when we fire at the same target at the same slope with a 122-millimetre Howitzer, for example, because the angle of impact with a mortar is very high, and that is why the dispersion pattern, if we confirm -- compare 122 Howitzer and a 120-millimetre mortar. The dispersion pattern will not really vary that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about the mortar.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the dispersion pattern with a mortar will increase if the target is on a rear slope. So is the answer yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it will increase.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If the ellipse decreases if the target that we're talking about is at the end of the ultimate range of the mortar, would in that situation the dispersion ellipse increase since the trajectory has a lower angle of impact?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it will increase more?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispersion ellipse at the end of the range, as represented by Vd and Vp, will increase.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, look at this map that the usher is holding. We're now looking at Prosecution Exhibit P10. Could you look at the following: On this map, Srdj is at 412 metres. The altitude of the Old City is 0.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or up to 50 metres, the highest parts of the Old City.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the altitude difference is that much. What is the height difference between that and the Old Town? It's about 800 metres, isn't it? So the slope from Srdj towards the Old City amounts to about 350 metres, a little bit over 350 metres, to the overall length of 800 metres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you permit me, none of the targets in the sector of Dubrovnik is on a rear slope in the way that I drew it, because it is on a front slope both for weapons and for observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please try to answer my questions. Is the altitude difference between Srdj and the Old City 112 metres and 50 metres altitude? So the Old City is at 0. If we take this total length of 850 metres, is the difference in height about 400 metres? All the targets that you are mentioning in your addendum 1 and 2 and which are, as you say, from 300 to 350 metres north of the Old Town or 100 or 150 metres west of the Old Town, are they all on a rear slope?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they are not on a rear slope.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, do you have this map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What do these horizontal lines mean marked by 400, 300, 100? What do these lines represent?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: These lines represent the altitude of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see in this area in which you are talking about 350 -- first of all tell us, since you are familiar with maps, what is the slope of the ground between two -- between two contours?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the density of the contours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you are an experienced gunner, so could you please count between 200 and 300, and you can see there are five contours and each one corresponds to 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terrain towards Srdj is very steep, and I think it is at least 40 -- at an angle of 45 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So each line represents a 20 metre drop in the terrain. Each contour represents a 20 metre drop.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This upper road, which is the Adriatic highway, it is the most northern road that we see to the north of the Old Town up to the Old Town, you can see four contour lines. So that is a drop in the terrain of 80 metres. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if those targets that you are talking about in the area between the northern walls of the Old City and the northern road, the Adriatic Highway, according to the map those targets are at a slope of 80 metres for the entire length between the northern walls of the Old City and the Adriatic Highway.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the targets which are 300 to 350 metres north of the Old City, or 100 to 150 metres away from the Old Town are at a rear slope.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those targets are primarily on flat terrain. You can very slightly speak about a rear slope. I've drawn what a rear slope is, and I've also toured those areas, and we cannot really take that to be as a rear slope from the point of view of the position of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, please take your ruler and measure how many metres it is from the northern walls of the Old City to the Adriatic Highway. At the end of the map, you have the scale.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about 12.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, please measure it.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can talk about 100 or 150 -- 150 to 180 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So on those 150 metres we have a slope, a drop of 80 metres, a descent angle of 80 metres.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to see here if it is a descent angle, because we cannot see the end of the contour lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, as an experienced gunner and a cartographer, as a person who toured that terrain a couple of weeks ago, please don't tell us that there are some -- there are no elevations there and that the ground does not slope from the top towards the Old City. Where do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. This is a speech. This is a speech or argument, that's all it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is descending into an argument. You put your questions, you get your answers, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I agree. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, at -- in the area from the Northern Adriatic to the northern walls of the Old City is there a descent of 30 per cent or is there not such a descent there? If you feel that the descent is not to such a degree, say so.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area is on a slope, but it's not as much as you say. It's a little bit undulating. You have an elevation and then you have a slope and then you have the highway. It's not a straight slope like I drew it, it's more of a curving surface. These are small areas, and overall we can say that it is a small back slope, but there is a large number of smaller features on that ground which are not represented on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, does this map have any elevation drawn into it between the northern walls of the Old City and the Adriatic Highway?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I suggest that we go on our first break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first morning break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, Your Honour, I would like to ask for a clarification and a correction in relation to my question. When we talked about paragraphs 20 and 21 of the basic report of Mr. Poje, this is page 26, line 10 of the transcript today, the transcript says is Mr. Poje's conclusion that Stradun constitutes a boundary of the lower range of the mortar, and the question was supposed to read as follows -- that's what the transcript was supposed to say, whether Stradun is the upper end of the range of the mortar. So could that please be clarified now for the sake of the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I must say I had rather understood you and the witness each to be speaking of the furthest range of the mortar, and I see the witness acknowledging the correctness of that. So the transcript is in error at that point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, we're going back to the question that we talked about a short while ago. So do you agree that in the area to the north of the Old Town there is a slope from the Adriatic road, which is the northernmost road from the Old Town before Srdj, and then all the way to the ramparts?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a slope, a relatively small one, but there is a slope which ascends from the Adriatic road towards Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When calculating the dispersion ellipsis in addendum 1 and in addendum 2, did you place in that area two potential targets, as it says anti-aircraft gun to the north of the Old Town and the starting point of the cable car?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave these --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not speak at the same time, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Poje, that for these two objectives you did not calculate the real increase in dispersion in view of the rear slope of the terrain? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not because the rear slope is very small, and in that area dispersion is decreased rather than increased because the target is below the horizon of the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question is, since you said to us awhile ago that if the target is on the rear slope, did you take into account the fact that dispersion is increased when the target is on the rear slope? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the dispersion ellipsis that you gave and that pertain to the PA gun to the north of the Old Town and again to the north of the Old Town the cable car, that the -- in real terms, the values are higher than what you gave in addendum 1 or 2?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I look at the slope only, then I did not take it into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Or, rather, the dispersion pattern which is realistically higher than the dispersion pattern shown in addendum 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispersion pattern is not bigger in real terms, although I did not take into account the slope of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If the slope of the terrain or, rather, the rear slope, as you said to us half an hour ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There's a difference. Counsel is saying rear slope. He's saying there isn't a slope or it's very minor. Counsel keeps on saying rear slope and he's saying there isn't. We have to some agreement here. He keeps on saying, "As you've just said a half hour ago rear slope." It's misquote from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, there is a difference in degree between you and the witness. He will accept that there is a slight rear slope in the area. You want to put to him questions that seem to assume that there is a much greater slope. Your proposition, though, that there is a slope seems to be accepted by him, and your proposition that there is necessarily a greater dispersion pattern when it's falling on a backward slope is accepted by him. It's merely a question of degree as to how steep the slope is or not. So I think you can leave out your statement that it's -- by expressly or by implication suggesting it's a steep slope and just deal with the question of what is the effect of the slope that you both agree is there, whatever its degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm very grateful for your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, let us disregard the question of how big the slope is. That question can be resolved very easily by looking at the map, and there will be opportunity to discuss that. We agreed that there is a slope; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a mild slope.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We agreed that dispersion ellipsis at the rear slope is increased in relation to the horizontal ellipsis.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an increase but a very small one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We agreed that you in your report did not take into account the fact that targets are on the rear slope.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as the rear slope is concerned, is there a border value in terms of whether a terrain can be considered to be one that can be described as a rear slope or another one as not being on a rear slope? Is there a definition; and if so, what is the definition?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as rear slope is concerned, I don't know what the definition would be. I don't know what the border would be either when, for example, a flat land would be considered as a rear slope at some point. We usually considered rear slope in relation to targets that are right behind a target as I described on that improvised sketch, something along those lines. This example that we are looking at now, after the Adriatic road, the terrain is a bit hilly. It goes a bit up and a bit down, but roughly speaking, from the Adriatic road towards the Old Town the terrain does descend a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The sketch that you drew, could you please sign it and could you please put the date on it, today's date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honour, I would like to tender it into evidence, please, as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit is D87.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I am just going to show you a calculation according to which the dispersion ellipsis is increased by 7 per cent in terms of length in the situation that we are discussing here. Do you agree with that assertion or not?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can be calculated. Well, I don't know. I cannot say anything just off-the-cuff, whether this 7 per cent figure is right or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, must not the degree of increase depend on the slope? If the dispersion pattern is measured in the horizontal plane, we know what it is. Simply because the shot is falling on a slope, the same dispersion pattern on the ground has a bigger area. That's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A slope like that, the dispersion pattern on the ground will be much bigger than if the slope is like that rather than horizontal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. I'm glad that we managed to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You explained that a long time ago. The problem I had is with your last question. You were putting it as though there was a figure, 7 per cent. That would only be true at one particular angle of slope.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was getting worried that I had misunderstood what this was all about. That's all right. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is something that will be dealt with during our proceedings in the future, so you will have the opportunity of hearing more about this. Has the witness been given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see from the transcript that my role has been taken over by Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this exhibit please be given a number. If a number has already been assigned and I was not aware of it, I do apologise. The sketch, the witness's sketch, was it assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I beg your pardon, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, we're now moving on to addendum 1 and addendum 2 to your report, and I remind you of what we said yesterday, what we established yesterday, and that is that platoons of company mortars are at Zarkovica, Dubac, and Strincjera. Is it correct that in your report you did not calculate dispersion from Dubac and from Strincjera?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I calculated it from Zarkovica, Bosanka, and Srdj, the ones contained in the addenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that from Strincjera, Bosanka and Dubac, in view of the geographic characteristics of the terrain and the position of the targets in relation to which you gave your opinion, is it true that it is only indirect firing that is possible?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as these targets are concerned, it is only possible to engage in indirect fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you say to us yesterday that as far as indirect fire is concerned, the dispersion pattern is increased, that is to say of the shells vis-a-vis the target?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the dispersion pattern in the case of indirect fire is certainly greater than that in the case of direct fire. How big the dispersion is is what columns 11 and 12 of the firing tables tell us, depending on the charge and depending on the targeting. I would like to add something to this because we did not actually finish a question yesterday. We did not deal with it completely. The difference in altitude between the firing position and the target is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, that is precisely one of the topics that we will be discussing today, the last one that you mentioned just now, and I am grateful to you for having brought it up yourself. So let us summarise this part. You did not take into account the positions of Bosanka, Strincjera, and Dubac as positions from which there is indirect firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. He did take into account Bosanka. It's right in the supplements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is unfortunately impatient. I was just about to ask the question that he did not take into account Bosanka, Strincjera, and Dubac as the ones from which indirect fire was opened. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If you're firing mortars, mortars are indirect fire weapons, so if he's looked at Bosanka as firing mortars from there, it's an indirect weapon, so he had to have taken it into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'll leave that to you, Mr. Petrovic, to sort that out. I won't start giving my theories.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would kindly ask the witness to respond to the assertion from the Prosecution that it is correct that with mortars you can only fire indirectly.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semi-indirectly is also possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to open direct fire from mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by indirect and semi-indirect firing?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indirect firing is done from weapons and from the positions from which you cannot see the target, and you aim at an auxiliary point, like surveyor poles, from where you observe the impact from an observation point or for any reason whatsoever there is no observation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you name firing from weapons from the position that you can't see the target and how do you define the semi-indirect firing?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you turned the barrel in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So any Howitzer can open indirect fire?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can open direct, indirect, and semi-indirect fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Concerning Howitzer, is it possible with a Howitzer also that are similar to the ones applying to mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Of course there are. In any case, whether we are talking about artillery weapons or mortars, the barrel is aiming towards the targets?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then how do you make a distinction between mortars by saying that allegedly its barrel is not turned towards the target and that that makes it a weapon that opens semi-direct fire?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would quote the artillery rule of firing, and I also included in my report what are the definitions of direct, semi-direct, or indirect firing. That is what I wrote in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's not waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you agree, I will move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, twice he's asked him what indirect and semi-direct fire was, twice he's stopped him from answering the question. Now the witness wants to explain and now they're stopping him again. The witness should be allowed to answer his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think there is clearly some confusion of terminology. Mr. Petrovic, it would certainly help the record and the proceedings if the witness went over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me to do it in this way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be that a mortar is a weapon with an indirect fire capacity, but that doesn't mean it can't be used to target a weapon that can be seen from the firing position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we accept what you say, then I think that we can wrap up this matter altogether as far as we are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be in the witness box and cross-examine me, next. I was merely reflecting what I had understood from the witness. And does that help you, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It does, but I think further elucidation would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the trouble is that the witness is using his terms in the strictly defined sense, and I think each of those that are listening may be listening to them in other senses, if you can understand that. I understand his evidence when I keep in mind his definitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, in addendums 1 and 2 to your report, let us identify the targets for which you made calculations of dispersion. First of all, in addendum 2, you are talking about anti-aircraft guns situated 100 -- 150 to 200 metres to the north from the Old Town. Asked the question posed by my learned colleagues on the 10th of May in this court, that is what you said exactly at 1726 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then you calculated the target marked as the starting point of the cable car structure. You said that it was 300 to 350 metres to the north from the Old Town. That is what you said in this court on the 10th of May at 1802 hours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, the anti-aircraft gun and the cable car approximately in the same direction vis-a-vis the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, in addendum 1 to your report, you mentioned the targets marked as Vrata Od Ploca. How far is that target Vrata Od Ploca from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a map would be helpful, but I think it's about 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be given Exhibit P10, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, could you please look at the map that I have given you, and you will have an opportunity to answer my colleague's questions later. Let me just say that the map marked P10 is the map tendered by the Prosecution, and it had been prepared by the defence mapping agency of the government of the United States, and as such it has been tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom the map a little bit, because we can't see the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So 500 metres to the east from the Old Town, can you please show us approximately where that would be?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that that is the area called Vrata Od Ploca.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the firing position was there, the one which was marked on the map prepared by the command -- defence command of the town of Dubrovnik, and we looked at those targets, and this firing position or mortar unit was marked, and that refers to the general area of Ploce.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this map, Exhibit P10, and you say that it's 500 metres to the east. These are the numbers - 53, 14, 127 - signifying streets. There is another feature, 147 -- 143. And can you please tell us at which of these locations would be this target that you made the calculation for?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
