utterances.text: The majority of those officers that I met at these firing exercises who worked for the centre had finished secondary artillery school in Zadar, and the military academy with a major in artillery in Zadar too. I even suppose that some of the units --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's not the question. That's not the question. Which academy in Zadar? Was it the artillery academy or one of the other academies that they were trained?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those officers and junior officers attended the artillery school centre according to plans and programmes for such training for artillery officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. And then the last quick area. Yesterday you were asked about the placement of a gun 15 metres from a wall, that if you had a barrel of an elevation of 45 degrees, you can move a gun 15 metres away from the wall and fire if it was a 15-metre high wall. So the distance and the height would be the same. And then counsel asked you if the elevation was over 45 degrees, could you move closer to the wall? Although it's possible to move closer than 15 metres to the wall, is it safe and practical to do so?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I don't quite understand your question, could you please repeat it for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If you have a 15-metre high wall and you have a mortar at 45 degrees facing the wall, the earliest that you can move the mortar back -- farthest back you can move the mortar would be 15 metres -- or the closest to the wall the mortar could be would be 15 metres so that it could still fire over the wall. And then counsel said could you raise the barrel and move the mortar closer? And you said yes. Is that safe and practical to do, moving closer to the wall with the mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The firing position of a mortar is not being selected to target only one target. It's being, rather, selected for multiple targets in an area. Today we looked at the map which showed 15, 16, or 17 targets, planned targets, and then the firing position selected is such that enables to engage all these targets from one firing position. For that reason, the minimal elevation is calculated and the minimal distance also to the obstacle that is facing the mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Last question: If you were less than 15 metres from the wall and due to a sighting error in the elevation you fire into the wall, what happens to that mortar crew?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the conclusion is quite clear; that they would hit themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how would you determine the minimum distance?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the firing tables and instructions for setting up firing positions describe the procedure for determining the lowest possible elevation and for the elevation of a cover. In this case, a building can serve for that purpose. And the firing even can be affected by an obstacle which is even lower than the one which is close to the weapon and is farther away. So you have to calculate this distance and I cannot tell you now offhand what the formula to be applied is. The deputy commander of a mortar battery or platoon is the one to determine that, by using an instrument which is called sitometer with which he can calculate the minimum distance from the edge of the cover or from an obstacle which is in front of a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal, and I'm pleased to tell you that the evidence you are to give is now at an end and you are free to return to your home. So thank you indeed. We will now adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
